text.text: Communication failures are repeatedly implicated in harmful experiences and outcomes in pregnancy care, especially in contexts of loss, yet little is known about how communication itself is represented in the institutional texts that shape expectations of care.
This study examines the extent to which communication is discussed, and how patient-healthcare professional interaction is framed, in publicly accessible UK discourse about pregnancy loss.
Two corpora comprising texts from seven medical organisations (120,383 words) and eight charities (224,481 words) were divided into healthcare professional-facing and patient-facing sub-corpora.
Frequency, semantic keyness, keyword and concordance analyses were conducted using Wmatrix7.

In medical discourse, language and communicative interaction were underrepresented, while speech acts associated with unidirectional professional activities such as advising, recommending and referring were overrepresented.
Compared with charity texts, medical outputs foregrounded clinical evidence, policy, risk and professional knowledge.

text.text: That communication is a significant factor in determining patient experience in this context has been recognised by the outputs of the UK's National Maternity and Neonatal Services Investigation (MNSI), led by Baroness Valerie Amos, which concluded in 2026.

One way to begin to answer this question is by looking at how communication between patients and professionals is currently represented in contemporary texts about pregnancy loss produced by organisations such as the NHS, and other influential public health institutions in the UK.

Employing purpose-built datasets, or corpora, comprising large numbers of publicly accessible texts on this subject, we use computer software to identify recurring, or statistically salient, language choices -an approach known as corpus linguistics (McEnery and Hardie, 2012).

text.text: We combine this with qualitative analysis drawing on concepts from critical discourse analysis (CDA) and communication studies, such as framing (Entman, 1993), in order to identify the understandings and perceptions that these linguistic patterns could reflect and reinforce in this context.

text.text: This combination of corpus linguistic and CDA approaches has previously been shown to offer a 'useful methodological synergy' through which to explore specific discourses, including in health communication contexts (Baker et al. 2008; see also Baker et al. 2020; Partington et al. 2013).

text.text: This article therefore adopts a corpus-informed, critical linguistic approach to investigating how communication between healthcare professionals and patients is framed in institutional discourses relating to pregnancy loss in the UK.

Two corpora were built which aimed to be representative of the publicly accessible institutional language of a) UK medical organisations; and b) UK-based charities, specific to the topic of loss during pregnancy.
These corpora were then analysed in terms of the following research questions: 1) To what extent is health communication (including language) discussed within these institutional discourses?
2) How is communication between patients and healthcare professionals framed?
This research is situated in the context of the growing body of work on health communication in applied linguistics and related fields.

As defined by Harvey and Adolphs (2011: 470), health communication covers 'a huge and diverse range of communicative activities touching on health and healthcare, ranging from personal accounts of health and illness and encounters with medical professionals through to health policy documentation and side effects information presented on drug packaging'.

text.text: This article examines written language used by prominent UK medical institutions and charities on their websites as examples of health discourse.

We examine these discourses from a critical standpoint, drawing on the CDA understanding of 'discourse' as a form of social practice which not only reflects underlying attitudes, or ideologies, but also serves to construct and reinforce them (Brookes, 2026: 323-4; Fairclough, 2003; Jones, 2013).

text.text: In this view, discourse 'constitutes a central activity to the practices of institutions related to health' (Brookes and Hunt 2021: 4).

text.text: As will be described in more detail in the next section, the discourses considered for the purpose of the present research are made up of written texts produced by UK organisations which a) share a common focus on pregnancy loss, and which b) are easily accessible to the public on their websites.

They can thus be compared with other forms of public health communication such as care guidelines (Pattison, 2006), charity reports (Abnett et al., 2025) and public health campaigns (Brookes et al., 2016).

text.text: Such texts are predicted to have implications for their target audiences in terms of the perceptions they construct or reinforce.

Public-facing health information texts may influence patients' expectations of, and engagement with, healthcare through their representation of health conditions and patients themselves (Brookes et al., 2016; Stanley et al., 2025).

text.text: At the same time, public health communication texts also represent healthcare practitioners and the institutions in which they work.

This representation can influence professional identities and self-concepts of healthcare practitioners, including understandings of how they should communicate with each other and with patients (Pattison, 2006; Sun and Chalupnik, 2022).

text.text: This article explores how both patients and practitioners are represented in the institutional discourses in question, specifically in terms of the roles they take in communication, and considers the implications of these representations for different target audiences.
Before outlining the data in the following section, we first introduce a useful theoretical concept underpinning this research.

The notion of 'framing' has been used differently in various fields including sociology, semantics, artificial intelligence and cognitive linguistics, but might broadly be defined as an effect or function of 'particular lexical and grammatical choices' which 'generates expectations and inferences in communication and action' (Semino et al. 2016: 3).

text.text: In their study of representations of cancer on social media, Semino et al. (2016) build on the account of framing given in Conceptual Metaphor Theory (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980) as 'a bias of conceptualisation' which has the power to influence how we think about and act on a situation.

text.text: To frame is to select some aspects of a perceived reality and make them more salient in a communicating text, in such a way as to promote a particular problem definition, causal interpretation, moral evaluation, and/or treatment recommendation for the item described. text.text: In this article, rather than focusing on how the experience of pregnancy loss is framed, we focus on the framing of communicative interactions between patients and healthcare professionals about pregnancy loss.
Our goal is to consider the potential ramifications of the framings under examination, for how practitioners and patients approach these communicative situations.
In order to investigate institutional discourse around pregnancy loss in the UK, two corpora were constructed.
The first of these -the 'Medical corpus' -consisted of web content and online documents about pregnancy loss from 7 prominent UK medical organisations (see Appendix 1; Table 1).

text.text: Since the research aims to identify possible implications of the language for public and practitioner conceptions of pregnancy loss care, texts were sampled on the basis of ease of accessibility and hence potential reach and impact.

Texts were sourced by searching for key terms in the websites of medical organisations such as the National Health Service (NHS), the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and the Royal Colleges of healthcare professions likely to be involved in pregnancy loss care.

Key terms (miscarriage, ectopic, stillbirth, pregnancy loss, baby loss, fetal loss, fetal death, termination) were chosen on the basis of previous research into common terminology surrounding pregnancy loss in the UK (Malory, Nuttall and Heazell, 2025).
text.formatted: Key terms (miscarriage, ectopic, stillbirth, pregnancy loss, baby loss, fetal loss, fetal death, termination) were chosen on the basis of previous research into common terminology surrounding pregnancy loss in the UK <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Malory, Nuttall and Heazell, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Only publicly accessible texts were collected, meaning that any content requiring professional membership and/or password access were not included in the corpus.
Where a webpage or document covered broader topics such as maternity care or reproductive medicine, only sections relevant to the focus of the analysis were collected.
This relevance was determined by the title and/or inclusion of two or more instances of at least one key search term in the body of the text.
The same sampling criteria were applied to texts covering related topics, such as the abortion of unwanted pregnancies and neonatal death (the loss of a baby in the first 28 days after birth).

The collected texts include patient information pages/leaflets, clinical guidelines, training materials/curricula for healthcare professionals, best practice papers, and reports from audits of clinical services.

This range is representative of this discourse-type and the multiple registers typically contained with it, including research findings, (fictional) case studies, FAQs, resource lists and contact details.
However, since our focus is on written text data, any videos or podcasts were not included.
In order to provide a point of comparison, a second corpus -the 'Charity corpus'was built using similar methods.
This corpus consisted of web content from 8 prominent UK charities on the subject of pregnancy loss (See Appendix 1; Table 2).

text.text: The search terms listed above were used to collect publicly accessible written content on this topic, with the resulting texts including both patient information guides or booklets, and guidelines for healthcare professionals, and again featuring case studies and contact lists along with detailed information and advice.

While this corpus does not contain the same range of text-types as the Medical corpus, this is again representative of this discourse, which is primarily focused on information and guidance for patients and their families.
As Appendix Tables 1 and 2 show, our corpora do not contain equal amounts of text from each organisation sampled.

text.text: The number of texts from each organisation varies, as does the length of these texts, reflective of the range of eligible content that was relevant to our topic from each source, as defined by our sampling criteria.
The analysis does not make claims about specific organisations, but rather the dataset as a whole, and findings must be interpreted in relation to the make-up of each corpus.
Finally, these samples are not exhaustive of the institutional discourse on pregnancy loss published online.
However, since our aim was to collect texts most likely to reach the widest audience, sampling prioritised accurate representation of the most prominent, or influential organisations.
The two resultant corpora contain 120,383 words (Medical corpus) and 224,481 words (Charity corpus), respectively.
While relatively small, these datasets are intended to be representative of these two types of health discourse for the purposes of corpus analysis.
However, the different audiences targeted within each corpus (see Appendix 1; Tables 1 and 2) poses challenges for comparison.

text.text: The role of third sector organisations means that the Charity corpus is dominated by texts aimed primarily at patients, families and the general public, with only a smaller number targeting healthcare professionals specifically.
By contrast, the Medical corpus is dominated by texts aimed at healthcare professionals, trainees, or commissioners, with a smaller number targeting patients and the general public.
To address this challenge, both corpora were divided into two sub-corpora, with texts categorised based on their function of information sharing: 'healthcare professional-facing' or 'patient-facing'.

Finally, concordance lines for each (sub)corpus were manually examined for those positive and negative keywords relating to communication, with a focus on the specific ways in which interactions between patients and healthcare professionals are framed in context.
These corpus linguistic methods allowed us to assess the extent to which communication is a topic within the institutional health discourses, and the way in which it is framed when it does appear.
Results from each phase of analysis are outlined in the following four sections.
In order to assess the extent to which the topics of language and communication are discussed in the Medical corpus (RQ1), a basic word frequency analysis was conducted using Wmatrix7.

The lemmas communic* and lang* are seen relatively infrequently in the 120,383word Medical corpus, with words such as communicate, communicating, communication appearing 32 times and mentions of language(s) appearing just 17 times.
This may reflect the under-privileging of communication as a factor in perinatal healthcare (see Malory, 2025).

This preliminary analysis shows that the semantic domain of 'Speech acts', definable as an utterance that serves a communicative function, occurs significantly more frequently in the medical corpus relative to general British English.
Examination of concordance lines for this domain shows words such as recommendation(s), advice, explain, report and referral tagged in this category.

On the other hand, both the domains of 'Speech: Communicative' (containing 'terms relating to spoken communication' (Archer et al, 2002: 23); e.g. talk, speak, communication) and 'Language, Speech and Grammar' (containing 'terms relating to language' (2002: 24); e.g. language, words, terms, read, interpreter) both occur significantly less frequently in the Medical corpus relative to general written British English.

text.text: While communication does appear, therefore, to be a topic within the medical discourse, this analysis suggests that certain kinds of communication (particularly those kinds carried out by professionals) are emphasised over others, and that the speech and language through which communication is achieved may not be a primary focus.

The type and nature of the communication described in this corpus, or the ways in which the different interactions which take place in this context are 'framed' (see Section 2), are therefore in need of closer analysis.

In order to compare how communication is framed (RQ2), the Medical Corpus was then compared to the 224,481-word Charity corpus, this time looking for positive keywords in order to examine the specific expressions at work in construing communication in each discourse (see Section 3).

This includes the use of the passive voice, as in 'you will be advised' or 'you may be offered', where it is the passive patient-recipient 'you' who is foregrounded in subject position, with the professional who advises or offers scans, grammatically absent from the clause altogether.

In other instances, both patient and professional are removed from attention: for example, 'methotrexate may be recommended', 'it is advisable', 'miscarriage is confirmed' do not attribute the implicit communicative (and interpretative) processes described by these verbs to any particular participant, and in some cases attribute this process to a 'test' or 'results' as opposed to a person who interprets and delivers information: e.g.
'results can confirm'.
This is also the case for nouns such as advice and follow-up, in which an interaction between patient and professional is implied but not made salient by the framing.

While the majority of communicative keywords characteristic of the texts produced by medical organisations for public audiences therefore again frame healthcare professionals in an agentive role in interaction with patients, this analysis raises a further consideration here concerning the explicitness with which this professional communicator is construed within patient-facing information.

Alongside the attribution of agency, the saliency with which (specific) healthcare professionals are represented as communicators at particular points in care has other implications for the patients who are recipients of such texts.
One notable exception to this framing pattern is reporting.

text.text: Notably, they are more active; simple (e.g. 'nurse might ask') and infinitival ('to say') verb forms, occurring in the active as opposed to passive voice (e.g. 'the hospital staff will tell you', rather than 'you will be told').

Through this framing, communicative agency is assigned to both patients and professionals using the same linguistic choices, with the specific participants involved in the interaction made salient in attention.
Framing of interaction therefore seems to exhibit key differences between the two patient-facing sub-corpora.

Firstly, patient-facing texts produced by charities more frequently frame the patient as an agentive communicator who shares, questions or describes their experiences; often through the same communicative processes attributed to the healthcare professional (e.g. talk, tell, say).
Patient-facing texts produced by medical organisations, on the other hand, typically attribute agency or power to the professional, except for in specific scenarios such as the reporting of risk.
This provides evidence that charities' discourses are more empowering in their more balanced framing of communication as reciprocal and bidirectional.

Secondly, medical organisations' outputs focus primarily on conveying a diagnosis, treatment or advice, with the professional often backgrounded, or implicit, as the communicator in a transfer of information to the patient (e.g. 'the results confirm').

By contrast, the charities' outputs regularly foreground individual healthcare professionals (e.g. sonographers, Section 4.2) as active communicators in specific interactions with patients (e.g. 'a clinician will talk you through').

In this way, patient-facing texts produced by charities can be seen as more transparent and accessible in their representations of typical interactions and what can be expected from professionals involved in care.

Comparing these two patient-facing sub-corpora has therefore revealed differences in both the types of communication being represented and the extent to which participants, as active communicators and respondents, are foregrounded through the language used.
This could have ramifications for patients and other members of the public who access these texts to better understand the experience of loss.

This study examined the extent to which communication is discussed in UK institutional discourses around pregnancy loss (RQ1), and how communication between patients and healthcare professionals is framed within these discourses (RQ2).
The findings reveal a consistent contrast between texts produced by medical organisations and those produced by charities.
In the Medical corpus, semantic domains relating to spoken communication and language were significantly under-represented relative to general written British English.

Communication was therefore predominantly construed as the transmission of professionally authorised information rather than as dialogue.
The keyword comparison reinforced this finding.

Words relating to dialogue between patient and professional (e.g. say, telling, hear, listen), were over-represented in the Charity corpus along with mentions of specific professional roles involved in key conversations.
Overall, charity outputs gave greater prominence to talking, listening, feelings, preferences, wording and patient perceptions.
Medical outputs instead foregrounded clinical terminology, evidence, policy, risk and professional knowledge.
The audience-matched keyword analyses clarified how this contrast manifested in texts aimed at different audiences.

Across healthcare professional-facing texts, those produced by charities again featured a greater emphasis on forms of written and spoken communication as part of clinical practice, including discussion of wording or delivery, and the needs and preferences of parents.
As well as giving less emphasis to communicative aspects of care, texts produced by medical organisations also featured a lack of guidance as to how they ought to be carried out by professionals.
Across patient-facing texts, key differences between medical and charity discourses related to the framing of specific types of communication.
Charity outputs represented both patients and professionals as communicatively active and more frequently identified (likely) individual participants in particular interactions.

In Medical outputs, characteristic communicative expressions, such as confirmed, advised, recommended and offered, foregrounded professional agency in these communicative scenarios, but typically did not identify the individual participants involved.
Patient agency was most clearly foregrounded in relation to reporting symptoms or concerns.

Taken together, these patterns frame medical communication as a largely unidirectional, and often impersonal, transfer of information, while charity discourse more often frames it as interpersonal, reciprocal, and emotionally consequential.
Several limitations qualify these conclusions.

The corpora are relatively small, unequal in size and restricted to publicly accessible written materials; they therefore exclude password-protected professional resources and spoken or multimodal content.
Corpus patterns cannot demonstrate how individual texts are received or establish direct effects on clinical practice.

Future research should examine whether these framings recur in training materials and clinical interactions, and should test their effects through interviews, observations and co-produced evaluations with healthcare professionals and people with lived experience.5.1.
Implications for healthcare professionals and professional bodiesInstitutional discourse contributes to defining what healthcare professionals are expected to know and do.
The Medical corpus constructs the professional's communicative role primarily as the transmission of clinical knowledge: someone who diagnoses, advises, recommends and offers treatment.
Far less attention is given to the professional as a relational communicator who listens, responds to emotion, explains terminology sensitively, elicits preferences, and checks understanding.
Communication is consequently positioned as peripheral to clinical expertise rather than as one of the means through which safe and compassionate care is delivered.

healthcare professionals themselves communicate in these ways, but it means that the institutional texts intended to guide them provide limited discursive support for recognising communication as a core component of their professional role.

Medical organisations should therefore integrate specific communication guidance throughout clinical guidelines, curricula, and patient pathways; rather than treating it as a separate or optional "soft skill".

Guidance should identify who is responsible for communicating information, specify the importance of listening and responding as well as explaining, address the emotional and interpersonal effects of wording; and require professionals to elicit language preferences, invite questions, and check understanding.
The greater attention paid to these practices in charity-produced professional guidance demonstrates awareness within that sector of the need for this guidance.

Charities should not, however, be left to compensate for omissions in authoritative medical discourse: responsibility for establishing communication as a clinical standard rests with the institutions that define and regulate professional practice.
framing identified in patient-facing medical discourses also has implications for what patients understand themselves to be entitled and expected to do.
When communication is represented principally through being advised, offered or told, patients are positioned primarily as recipients of professional knowledge.
Their communicative agency is most visible when they are instructed to report symptoms or risk indicators.

This creates a restricted model of participation in which the patient's role is to supply clinically relevant information and receive professional decisions, rather than to question, interpret, express preferences, or contribute experiential knowledge.

The prominence of risk and lifestyle discourse may further individualise responsibility for preventing adverse outcomes, while the backgrounding of professional communicators makes institutional responsibility less visible.
By contrast, charity discourses provide patients with a more explicit account of what interactions may involve, who will communicate with them and what they may wish to ask, say, share, or know.
Patient-facing information from medical organisations should therefore represent communication as an active, two-way process.
It should name the professionals involved, explain what patients can expect from them and legitimise questions and preferences.
